title: The Pharmacist Who Invented Modern Contraception
event_summary: Mexican chemist Luis Ernesto Miramontes, a 26-year-old research assistant working under Carl Djerassi and George Rosenkranz at Syntex Laboratories in Mexico City, synthesized norethindrone — the first orally active progestational compound. He performed the critical final step on October 15, 1951, using barbasco root yams harvested by Indigenous communities in Veracruz as the raw material. This molecule became the active ingredient in the first oral contraceptive pill, fundamentally altering human reproduction.
why_forgotten: Credit for 'the Pill' was overwhelmingly given to Djerassi (Austrian-American) and later to Gregory Pincus, who organized clinical trials. Miramontes, the Mexican national who physically carried out the synthesis, was largely erased from popular narratives — a pattern of attribution bias against Latin American scientists. The Indigenous knowledge of barbasco yam's hormonal properties, which guided the entire research program, was never acknowledged at all.
why_it_matters: Norethindrone enabled the oral contraceptive pill approved in 1960, which catalyzed the sexual revolution, women's mass entry into the workforce, declining birth rates across the developed world, and profound shifts in family structure. The global population trajectory, women's economic independence, and modern reproductive medicine all trace directly to a synthesis performed in a Mexican laboratory using Indigenous botanical knowledge — a convergence of contributions almost entirely obscured by Cold War-era scientific politics.
